newsitem.title: UK: LABOUR AND EMU - a no-win situation for sterling?.
newsitem.headline: LABOUR AND EMU - a no-win situation for sterling?.

text.p: Sterling is in a no-win situation whether or not Britain's Labour party -- widely seen as the government in waiting -- turns out to be as supportive of European monetary union as many in the market believe it is.
Financial analysts said on Thursday there were nagging doubts about how EMU-friendly a Labour government might be.

In addition, even a clear commitment to joining a single currency could hurt sterling as deficit cuts would be necessary to prepare for monetary union and this in turn was likely to hit economic growth, they added.

"The predominant influence on sterling in the second half of the year will be the market's concerns that the government, perhaps as part of the preparation for potential membership of EMU, will be running quite a tight policy stance," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ International in London.
"That could generate quite a sharp weakening of the economy in 1998, in contrast to the obvious strength this year, and could be the trigger for some significant profit taking."
A slowing economy would dampen market speculation of higher domestic interest rates -- a key factor in sterling's steep appreciation since last year.
The Conservative party, which has held power since 1979, is riven by internal divisions over whether Britain should join EMU, due to begin in 1999. An election must be held by May 22.
Labour, though not uniformly pro-Europe, appears to lack such deep ideological doubts, analysts say. But EMU participation under a Labour government is far from a done deal, the analysts said
"If Labour do win the next election...I think they'll make positive noises on Europe but they won't go the whole hog," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell here.
Even if Labour does want to take sterling into a single currency, entry will not happen overnight.

Analysts say the new government would have many big domestic issues to tackle even before embarking on the legislative changes needed for EMU entry. They include a possible mini-budget, constitutional reform and youth unemployment

And ahead of the election, no party will be happy with sterling so near its old Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) lower limit of 2.7780 marks, said Banque Paribas forex strategist Nick Parsons. The pound crashed out of the ERM in September 1992.
"ERM stands for one thing in the UK and that's the Enforced Recession Mechanism. I don't believe it would be sensible to fight the election with sterling back at those levels," he said.

If a Labour government is serious about boosting manufacturing and exports, it will be keen to engineer sterling lower. It is also likely to want slightly higher interest rates to dampen consumer spending and inflation pressures, he added.
But many say there is little mileage left in the British monetary-tightening cycle, and that will prove an added disincentive to holding sterling as other EU economies pick up.
"The thrust of monetary policy will turn away from the Anglo-Saxon economies toward the continental European economies," said Deutsche's Barr.
Countries keen to join EMU, such as Italy, have seen their currencies wobble lately as markets fret that monetary union might be delayed or its entry requirements failed.
One factor in sterling's strength has been its perceived safe haven status from EMU jitters. But analysts say that play has had its day, and such fears now tend to benefit the mark.
So even a clearly pro-EMU Labour may leave sterling cold.

"The markets may view Labour as somewhat more EMU-friendly," said IBJ's Hannah. "But given the considerable doubts about the timing of EMU I'm not sure that's necessarily going to benefit sterling that strongly in the short term."
